---
title: What black holes are
lang: en
free: true
---
A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so extreme that nothing — not matter, not light — can escape once it crosses a boundary called the event horizon. Beyond that boundary, the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, making departure physically impossible. At the centre lies a singularity, a point where known physics breaks down and density becomes theoretically infinite.

Black holes form when massive stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and collapse under their own gravity. If the stellar core that remains after a supernova explosion exceeds roughly three solar masses, no known force can halt the collapse, and a black hole is the result. Smaller remnants become neutron stars instead.

## Detecting the invisible

Because black holes emit no light, astronomers infer their presence indirectly. Gas and dust falling toward a black hole form a swirling accretion disk that heats to millions of degrees and radiates intensely in X-rays. Studying the orbital speeds of nearby stars can also reveal an invisible massive companion.

## Gravitational waves

When two black holes spiral together and merge, they shake spacetime itself, producing gravitational waves — ripples that travel at the speed of light. The LIGO and Virgo detectors first confirmed such a merger in 2015, opening an entirely new observational window on the universe.
